A Desk Jockey Passed on 40 Brown Bears. The 41st Charged

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The 41st Bear,” appeared in the September 1961 glitch of Outdoor Life.
  • Industry observers note that john Yenter turned away from a 20X spotting scope and looked me right in the eye.
  • I had just refused to go after the 39th bear that failed to meet my specifications, and John, my hunting partner, was again giving me a piece of his mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The 41st Bear,” appeared in the September 1961 glitch of Outdoor Life.

Industry observers note that john Yenter turned away from a 20X spotting scope and looked me right in the eye. He mentioned, “Bill, you’re absolutely crazy. Forget your foolish specifications and collect that bear. You’re acting like a decrepit old desk hand, not a hunter.”.

I had just refused to go after the 39th bear that failed to meet my specifications, and John, my hunting partner, was again giving me a piece of his mind. He never uses profanity, but he can do a blistering job without it. He had killed his bear like an expert, and now I, the junior member, was giving him trouble. Being six years older than I am, he felt perfectly justified in straightening me out.

It started months ago back in York, Pennsylvania, where my job — director of purchases for a large manufacturer of air-conditioning equipment — classifies me as a professional desk hand. I guess I look the part — gray, balding, and past several of man’s milestones.

According to recent reports, my business associates in Borg-Warner are fond of trying to decide whether I was born a penny-pincher, which made me a purchasing agent, or the other way around. While they were debating that issue, I was concentrating on a 60-day toughening-up routine of golf, bowling, hiking, and calisthenics to convert my body from paper-shuffling to hunting condition. This was important because John C. Yenter, a building contractor from Tyrone, Pennsylvania, and I were planning a Kodiak bear hunt. We had so completely enjoyed our polar bear hunt in Norway’s frozen arctic region (“Desk Hand vs. Polar Bear,” Outdoor Life, December, 1957) that John decided his work with West Virginia Pulp & Paper Organization could wait while we took a brown-bear hunt.

I wrote down some rigid specifications for my trophy brown bear and made a silent vow to live up to them. I wanted a male with a 10-foot-square hide, brown in color, a perfect pelt, and weighing 1,000 pounds or more.

Research indicated that Kodiak Island raised the largest, brownest bears, and a spring hunt would be my best bet for a trophy with a full-grown, unrubbed pelt. The idea was to get a bear fresh out of hibernation — before he ruined his pelt with mating-season fights or started to shed his winter coat. We scheduled our hunt for late April and early May, which appeared to be the prime time for Kodiak brownies.

According to recent reports, we met our outfitter, Alf Madsen, in Kodiak Village, on April 27. We knew that most Kodiak bear hunting is done from the salt-water bays around the island, but records show that more big bears are taken in the interior. So we were bound for Karluk Lake, in the center of the southern part of the island.

According to recent reports, the flight up the valleys, around and between the snow-covered mountains, was a sight so beautiful that we almost forgot we were in a little single-engine pontoon plane and at times many miles from any water to sit down on. We were in camp and ready to hunt on the morning of April 28.

According to recent reports, our camp consisted of one frame cabin, one tent cabin, and an outhouse, without door, 100 yards north on the main bear trail. All the camp equipment, including two outboard boats for lake travel, had been flown in.

According to recent reports, karluk Lake looked a lot like one of the fjords of Norway. The blue water of the lake was now entirely clear of ice, but there were deep snowdrifts on the mountain peaks above the lake. If we’d never seen a bear, the wild beauty of the place would have repaid me for the trip in full.

Sources indicate that we started the hunting campaign with all energy, and in two days we saw and classified 16 bears. I refused to stalk any of them because they failed to meet my specifications. John eventually suggested that I was displaying the stubbornness of a mule, rather than the calm judgment of a purchasing agent.

Our guides were by reputation the best on the island, and they soon proved that they deserved their standing. Some would call them Aleuts, but in reality they were members of the Koniaga Tribe, which has been considerably diluted by the Russians who owned the island until we bought Alaska from Russia in 1867. Our guides were proud of their Russian and Koniaga lineage, but they’re loyal United States citizens.

Recent findings suggest that my guide was Grishka Nicoli, and John’s was Nick Malutin. These guides spoke their native Koniaga language, which is spoken only and not written. They also spoke fluent Russian and awkward English. They spend about three months of the year as hunting guides and four months as commercial salmon fishermen. For the rest of the year they’re Koniaga gentlemen of leisure. Like my hunting partner John Yenter, the guides were convinced that I was entirely too meticulous in my trophy specifications.

The only encouragement I had came from Kim Clark, who had become a very key part of our expedition. His full name was Webster Kimberly Clark, and he was a refuge biologist employed by the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Kim had been reared in Greenfield, Massachusetts, had studied at the universities of Michigan, Massachusetts, Missouri, and Yale. He has a Doctor’s degree. Clark had done a vast amount of field research and had become one of the top authorities on North American bears. He was stationed on Kodiak Island by the federal government to study Kodiak bears.

Kim Clark had read my stories in Outdoor Life.* When Kim learned from outfitter Alf Madsen that I was planning a Kodiak hunt, he met me in Kodiak Village and asked if he could join the group to observe and record the data on bears killed. We were glad to have a man of his ability and knowledge.

During the early part of our stay on Karluk Lake, Kim worked alone and permitted us to hunt as hunters, not as scientists. He was a great addition to our expedition, because his lectures at night permitted us to do practical field work the next day in connection with our hunt. Between hunting, field and night classes, we were extremely well occupied.

Had it not been for Kim encouraging me to stick to my specifications, I might have given up. He encouraged me because accurate field data on a major male brown bear just out of hibernation is apparently very scarce.

By the third day my partner John was adjusting his own specifications to suit the bear that was in sight. We were glassing a brownie on the shoreline across the lake, and through the glasses it looked good — perfect hide, pleasing color, but slightly under my requirements as to size. John wanted it.

In a few minutes we were on our way across the lake, approaching very quietly so as not to alarm the bear. We landed several hundred yards from the bruin, and John started stalking the animal with his guide. In spite of the skill they displayed, the bear caught the man smell. He was on his way up the mountainside before John could shoot. He and Nick stood on the shore watching the occasional motion of a bush which indicated that the bear was going higher and away.

In a recent development, the bear was 150 yards from the lake shore when he came into a little opening in the brush where we could see him. At that point he made the biggest and last mistake of his life. He stopped and looked back. At that moment John fired. The bear fell. Two more shots finished him completely. John’s performance was a credit to him, to his .375 H. & H. Winchester, Model 70 rifle, and its Bausch & Lomb scope sight.

It was without question a major bear, the color was excellent, the 8½-feet-square hide was prime and perfect. John was a thoroughly happy hunter.

With his bear hide strung up to dry, John concentrated on the wonderful trout fishing near camp, with time out now and then to think up some fresh criticisms of my ideas about a proper trophy.

Sources indicate that at the end of the ninth day we sized up the situation and found that we had glassed 40 bears, killed one. I was still holding out for a bigger and better one.

Recent findings suggest that the weather was perfect for the first three days, which was probably why we saw so many bears. There was rain every day after that, and visibility was often too poor for good work with binoculars. There’s no climate on Kodiak, just a vast assortment of unexpected and undesirable weather.

When we started out the 10th morning, we found that what had been rain at the lake camp during the night had been snow above the 1,500-foot level on the mountain. In spite of that, our hunting began early, and at 8:30 we saw a bear that looked very interesting. He was a mile from the lake shore, 1,600 feet higher, just above the new but temporary snow line.

In a recent development, trying to get a better look at the bear, we moved up the bed of Cottonwood Creek. This took us out of sight of the bruin momentarily, but we knew exactly where he was because the snow line established his elevation and the pass made in the mountains by the creek marked his location the other way. Yet, an hour’s looking from our newly introduced position failed to locate him.

We then climbed up high on the right bank of Cottonwood Creek, and from there we glassed constantly until noon. We felt sure that the bear was there because we certainly would have seen him if he’d walked away.

At noon we abandoned that position and moved to a spot across the lake, a mile farther away, which gave us a better perspective and a view of more of the ground area. We took turns eating and resting, but we were constantly looking. The rain returned in full force and it was a very uncomfortable situation.

We never saw a sign of the bear until 4 o’clock, when suddenly he stood up and was in plain view again. It was now evident that we’d first seen him when he finished his morning feeding, and he’d bedded down for the day. Now he was up feeding again.

Sources indicate that after a few minutes of careful observation, the guides decided that this bear would meet every point in my specifications. This was a fine display of skill on the part of the guides and is something I could never hope to duplicate. To the inexperienced, a bear two miles away through a 20X Bausch & Lomb telescope is just a bear, but my guide was able to classify him very accurately as to sex, size, and condition.

I knew enough by now to trust this guide’s judgment, and in a few minutes we were on our way back across the lake to start the stalk.

Before we reached the far shore the clouds had dropped so low that the mountains were completely obscured.

Industry observers note that since John had killed his bear, we decided that he’d stay with the boat and the two guides would accompany me on the climb up the mountain. It took a few minutes to strip for action, which meant down to heavy underwear, a sweat shirt, rain suit, and hip boots. This sounds like unusual mountain-climbing equipment, but the first mile of our climb would be accomplished by wading up the creek. It was much easier that way than climbing through the murderous alder thickets on either side.

By 5:30 we’d accomplished the most difficult part of the climb and were at about the same height as the bear and 500 to 800 yards to the right of him. At this point we climbed out of the creek and dived into the alder thicket. All alder thickets are nasty, but this one was the worst that I’d ever seen.

Industry observers note that soon we picked up a prominent bear trail, a path so worn that one of the guides called it “a bear highway.” It was obviously the main bear trail on that particular mountainside, and we felt sure that my bear was on it. We had no idea which way he was traveling, so it was possible that we’d meet him at any moment. It was also possible that he’d park a few yards off the trail to observe and properly take care of anything that might be using the bear highway. It’s this kind of thinking that prevents daydreaming on brown-bear stalks.

Grishka, who was in front of me, explained that he’d lead and watch ahead. Nick would bring up the rear and watch behind us and to the sides of the trail. I was free to watch any angle that suited my fancy. I think this was a polite way of telling me that they didn’t trust my powers of observation.

In a recent development, I was planning what I’d do if certain things happened. I realized that any shooting would be at very close range because of the thick alders and the heavy fog. While my guides were both carrying .348 Winchesters with open sights, I was carrying a .375 Winchester with a Bausch & Lomb scope. No scope is ideal equipment for a quick shot at 10 yards, and I wished for an old-fashioned V notch and front post.

Nick must have been reading my mind. He said, “Bill, if we meet the bear and you have trouble with your rifle, just throw it down and grab mine. I’ll be right behind you.”.

In a recent development, nothing could have done me more harm than that speech. I knew now that he had no more confidence in my equipment than I had, and I was scared stiff. I had enough acid in my stomach to pickle a ton of iron castings.

We soon came out into the little open spot on the mountainside that we’d marked as the location of the bear when last seen almost two hours before. This clearing was about 100 feet in each direction — no alders, just dead grass almost knee high. We spent 20 minutes searching the open area and forcing our way into the brush around the edges, trying to pick up a trail or some sign of the bear.

It has been revealed that suddenly my head was gripped by Grishka, a powerful man but only five feet tall. He pulled my head down to his level, slapped his wet face against mine. Pointing to the right, he whispered in my ear, “Bear there. Shoot!”.

In a recent development, about 75 yards away, through a little opening in the brush, I could see a dark spot. It could have been a bear. As I dropped to one knee, my perfect guide braced his knees to my back to steady my position. His 9X binoculars were tight to his eyes and just above my head as he watched the bear.

Industry observers note that when I picked up that brown spot in my 2½X scope, I couldn’t tell whether it was a bear or not. If it was, I couldn’t for the life of me see which way he was pointing.

In a whisper, I asked Grishka, “Which end is the head on?”.

It has been revealed that after a full minute’s careful observation through his glasses, he put his mouth to my ear and said, “Other end. Shoot!”.

That concise data from Grishka was fed through my fire-control center down to the trigger finger, and my gun fired. I was so excited I didn’t hear the report of the rifle, nor was I conscious that there was any recoil. But I did hear the bullet hit something, and then a fraction of a second later I knew it was a bear. He roared his complete disapproval of the whole situation.

Sources indicate that then it seemed that the brown bulk went up in the air several feet. An instant later it was on the ground and for a split second was completely still. At that moment I fired my second shot, and the bear’s reaction to that was a quick lunge to the right, toward the alders. I fired my third shot as he disappeared.

Grishka had remarked the first shot was good, but I didn’t see how he could possibly know. The bear had disappeared into the brush just as though he hadn’t been touched.

In a recent development, both guides were now running as hard as they could to the right — in the same general direction the bear was going when we last saw him. It was quite obvious that they were attempting to get ahead of the bear before he reached the creek bed, which was 600 yards away. I caught them swiftly and stayed right with them, not due to any bravery on my part, but simply because it was obviously much safer to stay close to them and their two rifles.

In a recent development, our travel in the next few minutes was parallel to that of the bear, and we could follow his location by the noise he made. I thought — and hoped — that the amount of noise was due to the fact that he was badly wounded, running blind and knocking brush to one side.

Recent findings suggest that A few seconds later we were on the edge of the creek where we could look down a steep bank to the water 100 feet below. Then I realized that the noise of the bear was not to my left, as it had been, but almost back of me and getting closer. I turned to face the noise. A second later that bear came into sight less than 20 yards away.

According to recent reports, it was the most stirring sight a thrill hunter could ever hope to see. That bear was coming at us at top speed, and it looked as though he knew exactly what he was going to do when he got there.

I slammed the gun to my shoulder and looked at the bear in the scope sight. The contour of the ground was such that I could see the back of his neck, so I selected a spot where the neck joins the shoulders. The crosshairs settled on that spot. I tightened on the trigger, adding pressure and waiting for the recoil.

Recent findings suggest that but the bear rolled dead as Caesar before my rifle went off. I lowered the weapon still cocked and loaded. I never have felt so cheated in all my life. In another 1/10th of a second I could have been the Man Who Stopped the Charging Brownie.

Later examination showed that the first shot had gone very effectively into his side just back of the ribs, forward under the spine, just grazing it, cutting the main blood vessels just back of the heart. Clearly the bear had been too far gone to make a determined charge. He was only making a blind run with his last spark of life, and we happened to be in his path.

That bear was coming at us at top speed, and it looked as though he knew exactly what he was going to do when he got there.

According to recent reports, I examined the bear closely, and was glad that I’d stuck to my specifications. It was a male, the color dark brown, the hide in perfect condition, and the size was enough to flatter any desk hand. It was the 41st bear we’d seen on this trip.

Recent findings suggest that suddenly I realized that it was beginning to get dark. We’d have to leave the bear and return the next day to do the skinning. I was worried about what might happen to the hide overnight, but Grishka noted, “We leave strong man smell here. Nothing bother.” With a grin he added, “The strongest thing here is white-man smell of your sweat shirt. We leave it.”.

Recent findings suggest that I peeled off the shirt and he tied it to a limb above the bear. When we returned the next morning the shirt and the bear were there and nothing had bothered it.

The guides, Kim Clark, and I left camp early next morning and climbed the mountain to skin the bear. John remained in camp. He and the cook, Pete Unger, had planned a fishing trip.

According to recent reports, kim was keenly interested in the bear from our description so we went in loaded with camera equipment, scales, surgical instruments, test tubes, and specimen bottles. Very few Kodiak bears have ever been accurately weighed and examined, and this is especially true of big bears just out of hibernation.

My bear was an ideal specimen for studying the effects of hibernation, because he evidently had just come out of that lethargic state. The stomach was found to be about 1/10 full, and the contents weighed 16 pounds. Carefully separated and weighed, we found that the contents were 55 percent blue-joint grass, 20 percent nettle, 20 percent wild celery, and 5 percent poque, which is a parasitic growth on the roots of the alders. There was no animal matter present.

The intestine was then examined and the length was accurately determined to be 77 feet 6¾ inches. It was then split from end to end for internal examination. There was no food in it. This indicated two things: first, that the bear had not been out of hibernation long enough for food to pass through the stomach into the intestine, and second, that he had gone into hibernation with the intestine completely empty, which conformed to the generally accepted theory. Further examination revealed there wasn’t a sign of ulcer, scar, scab, or scale in the stomach or intestine.

We also observed that there were no parasites of any kind in the entire digestive tract. This is one of the strange results of hibernation, because this bear during the six months of feeding eats carrion of all kinds, specializing in dead fish. He also digs up and eats worms, insects, and roots. When winter comes, he’s literally and actually a fur coat full of worms. There are thousands of them, including 10-foot-long tapeworms. The bear knows instinctively that he cannot go into hibernation with any food in his body; it would ferment and cause serious trouble before spring.

So when winter approaches he goes on a bedtime diet of certain plants and berries. Then, after a few days of fasting, he’s completely empty. The worms go with the food, and he goes to sleep physically clean. His stored body fat keeps him going till spring.

It has been revealed that every piece of this bear was carefully weighed. He weighed 840 pounds at the time he was killed. Kim Clark figured his weight when he was fattened for hibernation in the fall would have been about 1,300 pounds.

His age was estimated at ten years. The rough field measurement of the skull indicated a Boone and Crockett rating of 28½, against the world record of slightly above 30 inches. Unless the skull shrinks more than an inch during the drying period that must precede official scoring, the trophy should rate a place on the Boone and Crockett record list. This was in every respect an outstanding bear. I learned a lot from him, and much more from Kim Clark.

The skull and all the data collected were sent to Dr. Robert Rausch, Arctic Health Research Center, Anchorage, Alaska, where it became a part of their records.

Read Next: We Stalked a Cannibal Brown Bear That Was Trying to Kill a Cub.

According to recent reports, we were glad to work with Dr. Kim Clark and Dr. Rausch, but in a way it was unfortunate. I can’t enlarge on the size of this bear as the years roll on and the hunt becomes a fond memory. This is one Kodiak that will never experience any post-mortem growth.

*H. L. Consley, who has become known to Outdoor Life readers as the Desk Hand, is the author of “Desk Hand in the Yukon,” in the January, 1956, concern; “Desk Hand Afloat,” November, 1956; “Desk Hand vs. Polar Bear,” December, 1957, and “Desk Hand in the Arctic,” August, 1959.

#79697. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1699 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Recent findings suggest that gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to proposal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Recent findings suggest that gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to proposal. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

It has been revealed that roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

In a recent development, for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

It has been revealed that northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and initiative ahead.

According to recent reports, the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

It has been revealed that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

Sources indicate that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with latest designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

In a recent development, food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

According to recent reports, successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

According to recent reports, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

In a recent development, I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

Industry observers note that we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

Sources indicate that the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

Industry observers note that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

It has been revealed that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

#79694. Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2918 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry.
  • It was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic.
  • Right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry. I wanted to get all packed up and then go in the hot tub first thing! That sounded like a wonderful way to start off the day. Last night I managed to coordinate a ride out of town with a few other hikers. The same kind man, Al, who we had breakfast with the other morning offered to drive a group back to the trailhead. About 5-6 hikers are getting back on trail at a road about 38 miles further south than where we’re getting back on trail. Al’s wife actually drove all of those hikers back to trail. Then Al was going to pick up Woods, Strix, and Leaf before coming to pick up Slide and myself around 9AM. That gave us plenty of time to go in the hot tub, shower, and have a little breakfast before hitting the trail.

It was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic. Slide and I soaked in there and then I took a final shower before we would be dirty hikers once more. The last couple of days off have been really nice. I needed the time to get some work done, and the trail needed some time to soak up all of the rain. I figure it we will still be dealing with the impacts of the storm for a little while, but hopefully it will be nothing in comparison to what it would have been like yesterday and the day before. After my shower I had a piece of pizza leftover from last night. Then I packed up the rest of my things and got ready to hit the road. We had talked about maybe walking down the road to the empanada place for breakfast. I absolutely love empanadas! But they didn’t open until 9AM and I didn’t want to make anyone wait for us, so we decided against it.

Right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up. We loaded everything into Al’s truck and talked with everyone as we got ready to go. Strix has been dealing with some foot pain and is going to get dropped off right down the street to try and hitch into the larger town of Payson. Woods and Leaf are going to continue south on the trail just like us but will go into town sometime tomorrow from the highway crossing in 38 miles. That way they can hopefully link back up with Strix, and all continue on together from there. Slide and I are going to continue another 71 miles hopefully in the next 3 days and will head into the town of Payson in the evening. That will help to break up the next section of trail a little bit better so that we don’t have to carry as much food.

A bridge that the trail crossed over in the early evening.

In a recent development, the ride to the trailhead took about 30 minutes but we got there eventually. It was so incredibly nice of Al to offer us a ride. And he made sure that we all had his phone number in case anyone needed some help over the next couple of days. That was really sweet of him. Then we were back on trail once more! It feels really good to be back at it after another double zero to avoid bad weather here in Arizona. We have now taken 5 zero days in the 17 days that we have been hiking the trail, which sounds absolutely crazy. It is in stark contrast to the way that Slide and I both hiked last year on our CYTC hikes. But we have the time to do it and hiking in that weather would have been really miserable. If not seriously dangerous. There are a couple different river crossings that we will have to go through tomorrow and the next day which would have hazardous or even impassable during the heavy rain. I’m curious to see how deep they will be only a couple of days after the rain has passed.

Almost immediately when we began hiking south, we encountered patches of mud and areas where the trail was almost completely flooded. For the first couple of miles, we managed to navigate around the wetter sections while still keeping our feet dry. But that didn’t last long. Eventually there were areas where the trail was under about 4-5 inches of water consistently, and there was no good way around it. I was pretty happy though that the trail was wetter than it was muddy. Areas like this will often get a thick mud that sticks to your shoes and cakes on heavily. Walking in mud like that for miles can make your ankles and feet incredibly sore just from the weight of the mud alone. Slipping and sliding in mud can also make my hips and knees hurt, depending on how bad the mud is. At least the trail today was much more wet than it was muddy.

Sources indicate that A happy little mushroom just off the trail. All of the plants have been loving this rain.

When we were about 5 miles into the day the trail crossed over a dirt parking lot and trailhead. There were some large boulders surrounding the parking lot, so Slide and I decided to stop off there and enjoy a quick break. We’re only planning to hike around 20 miles today, so there is no need to rush. Woods and Leaf were somewhere behind us as well and it sounded nice to let everyone catch up. I was surprised how much mud and dirt was already coating my legs after only a handful of miles of hiking. The two of us hung out there for a while and then continued along. And right as we were leaving, I could see at least one of the girls approaching off in the distance. They weren’t far behind!

Caked in mud and dirt, only 5 miles after leaving town.

Sources indicate that from there the trail continued through a forested area and we began to descend gradually. I could hear the loud roar of water off in the distance and began to wonder if we would be crossing the river that I could hear. Only a couple of miles after the trailhead where we had taken a break, we were now approaching a very large river. The trail did exactly what it always does when it requests you to cross a river. It descended all the way down until the trail disappeared and only the river laid before us. We had no choice but to cross it. The water looked deep and quite fast moving. I was not exactly eager to plunge into the freezing cold water. Slide on the other hand got right into the water and began to cross it. It’s always nice to gauge the water level on someone else before you also have to go through the water. We crossed right at the trail crossing and I could see the water rise to Slide’s upper thighs. He’s pretty tall so I knew that they water was going to be right up to the bottom of my shorts.

A river that we had to cross this morning.

I only had one trekking pole out which certainly wasn’t adequate for this crossing. The water was deep and very fast moving. With only one trekking pole I was not nearly stable enough. Plus, of course I was trying to record some videos of us crossing the water. I was glad that Slide was there on the other side. Otherwise, I would have probably had to pull my other trekking pole out to secure myself in that final stretch of the river crossing. But Slide just got back into the water and extended a hand to help me across that last little bit of river. Even though we had just stopped for a break less than an hour prior, we still decided to sit down there beside the river. I had a bunch of rocks in my shoes from crossing the river, and the girls likely weren’t far behind. They had each other so I wasn’t too worried about them. But they both are significantly shorter than Slide and me, so it seemed nice to wait around for them just in case.

Slide helping Leaf across the river.

We sat there beside the river for a while, waiting to see if the girls arrived. And just as we were thinking about packing up and continuing along, I could see one of the girls crest over the hillside on the other side of the river. So, we decided to wait just a bit longer to let them get across. The first person to appear was Leaf, and we gave her some guidance for crossing the river. It was really deep though so Slide wound up just going over to her to help. He got into the river and met her about halfway through to help bring her to the other side. Then she joined us on the shore, and we sat and talked with her for a bit. In hindsight, I’m so glad that we waited for her. Because neither Slide nor I realized that the other hiker Wood’s had actually done a road walk earlier on in the day, which meant she was no longer heading in this direction. If we had continued on, then Leaf would have been stuck going through the fast-paced river alone. Knowing that no one else was anywhere close by behind her. I’m sure she would have been alright, but I was glad that we stuck around.

The sign by the trailhead when we finally got off the dirt road and reconnected to the AZT.

Recent findings suggest that before we headed out to continue along, we told Leaf that we were hoping to go around 20 miles. Hopefully she will go the same distance, and we can all camp together later this evening. She came out here to meet up with this group and hike with everyone, and now she’s basically alone. She’ll be able to link back up with everyone tomorrow, but it would be nice for her to not have to be alone on trail tonight. From there I wasn’t sure what to expect along the trail. That river crossing was a complete surprise to me, so who knows what is up ahead of us now. We wound up climbing for a while to get up and out of the area where we crossed the river. Once we got up top of the climb, the trail was completely dry and the trail turned in a double wide dirt road. Leaf had pointed out to us that the trail actually crossed over a road that we could continue along for a little while. It would wind up reconnecting with the AZT but might give a reprieve from any possible mud.

The section of trail that we were hiking through just before dark was really beautiful.

In a recent development, after a mile or two we arrived at that dirt road crossing and decided to continue along the road as well. It sounded like a nice way to get a handful of miles in without too much struggle. The road was really nice and quite dry which was delightful. We walked through a bunch of different logging operations alongside the road. Trees were piled high in preparation of them being transported somewhere. We even walked by a logging camp with a bunch of recreational vehicles. I’ve heard about guys camping out and living at these types of logging operations. There were generators running and we saw a couple of guys and a dog running around. I wonder if they will have to hold off on logging for a while after all of the rain.

The sun beginning to set as we continued along the trail.

The road had a lot of long hills for us to climb and descend, but eventually we began going downhill continuously for a while as we got closer to the AZT. Then we passed by another trailhead parking area and turned right to get back on the trail. The trail began descending rapidly once we reconnected to it. And we went right past a junction for some kind of mine that you can walk to right off the trail. Some hikers left comments indicating that it was a great place to hide out in bad weather. But we decided not to explore the side trail down to it today. We’ll be hiking until after dark this evening most likely and didn’t need to get sidetracked. We did stop off for another break though to put some more layers on as it was getting later. And we hoped that if we sat for a break then Leaf might catch up to us as well. Both of us really wanted her to catch up so that she wouldn’t have to camp alone tonight.

Filtering water on the AZT with my platypus QuickDraw filter.

It has been revealed that the area that we were hiking through had numerous trailheads scattered throughout it, so we actually wound up seeing some day hikers not long after that. The trail also followed along a creek for a handful of miles toward the end of the day. It was great to have endless access to water if we needed it. We wound up stopping off and filling up on water sometime around 5PM, just so that we wouldn’t we wouldn’t have to worry about it for the rest of the night. And not long after that, the trail crossed over yet another trailhead. This one had a trail register as well, so I decided to leave a note for Leaf. I told her how much further we planned to go for the night in case she was close behind us and was hoping to camp together as well. Then we continued on with only a handful more miles to go for the day.

Standing up from a final break before we continued on into the dark.

Recent findings suggest that someone built this rock fort right next to the trail. I wonder how long it’s been there for.

It has been revealed that the trail began to climb gradually after we left that trailhead. Which meant that we got wonderful views of the sunset as it began to light up the sky. It’s pretty typical for us to stop off and enjoy one final break before the sun goes down. Especially if we are hiking somewhere with great views of the sunset. This was too perfect to pass up. When we did get going again, we came across some cows that were hanging out right on the trail. I always feel bad for scaring the cows. We try to talk nicely to them when we go past, but most of the time you wind up scaring the cows either way.

The sunset this evening was incredible. It’s always my favorite time of the day!

Eventually the sun went down, and we continued on in the dark for a little while longer. The area that we were hiking through did not seem like it was going to accommodate our need for a camp spot. So, when we finally did turn a corner and see a fairly flat area we decided to take advantage of it. There were some cow pies on the ground, and it wasn’t the best spot I’d ever seen, but it would work for tonight. The two of us got our tents set up and were hopeful that any minute now we would see Leaf’s headlamp coming around the corner. But that actually never happened. She must have stopped off for the night before the sun went down. Once my tent was set up, I got comfortable and had a little bit of dinner. Then did my stretching and a little editing in my tent before calling it a night.

No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (395 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • According to recent reports, “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • Industry observers note that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is promptly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

According to recent reports, “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

Industry observers note that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

It has been revealed that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

In a recent development, once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Recent findings suggest that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

#79691. Trophy Deer Hunting Is a Trap

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1054 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Trophy Deer Hunting Is a Trap

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Trophy Trap,” was originally published in the November 2006 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • According to recent reports, it was almost 40 years ago that the first whitetail came into my life.
  • Recent findings suggest that finally, I had entered the cadre of hunters who had taken a whitetail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Trophy Trap,” was originally published in the November 2006 issue of Outdoor Life.

According to recent reports, it was almost 40 years ago that the first whitetail came into my life. I dropped him on a granite ridge in New York’s Hudson River Valley, where, on a clear day, you could see the Empire State Building 40 miles away. The buck was only a forkhorn, but I was beside myself with excitement.

Recent findings suggest that finally, I had entered the cadre of hunters who had taken a whitetail. In those days, that feat often took some doing.

Sources indicate that back then, we knew next to nothing about white­tails. I worked as post forester and wildlife biologist for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point for eight years in the late ’60s and early ’70s, and one of my jobs was to manage the hunting program on the academy’s 16,000 acres in southern New York. I recall seeing large scratch marks under trees where some animal had pawed away leaves, but I had no clue what had done it or why. And neither did any­one else I talked to.

Then came fresh research as modern wildlife man­agement started to steamroll along, and we learned that those pawed areas were spots that somehow were linked to whitetail bucks before and during the rut. Now we call those disturbed areas “scrapes,” as every whitetail hunter from age 8 to 80 knows. Along with the research came the inevitable desire to “improve” whitetails and grow bucks with bigger and bigger racks. Studies on nutrition and genetics unearthed the means to grow super bucks. Intensive management was suddenly the name of the game around the country. People devel­oped genetically altered monster bucks, put up fences to contain them and began to sell their semen for about as much as my pickup truck cost. Since then breeding has become major business. And in some circles, hunting has become a matter of horn inches rather than the experience itself.

Am I complaining? Not at all. In fact, some good pals of mine run commercial whitetail preserves where intense management produces significant racks for their clients. That’s their business. And it’s here to stay. I simply see it as a sad commentary when we focus on the size of the rack rather than the smells, sights, and sounds of a damp oak forest and the raucous cries of jays and crows. Everything in the woods contributes to the total experience — and if a spike or forkhorn buck shows up, then you can be proud to flip off the safety, squeeze the trigger and smile all the way home.

Sources indicate that happily, this massive-buck syn­drome hasn’t affected everyone yet. Plenty of hunters, young and old, are still thrilled to down a forkhorn buck, but upcoming management concepts threaten the option of taking younger bucks. Biologically speaking, it’s indeed smart to let the younger bucks in some habitats live another year or two. My problem with the new techniques is that we continue to focus on the size of the antlers.

Proponents of associations that pro­mote minimum antler restrictions steadfastly insist they aren’t focusing on trophy deer. But it seems to me that when you require a deer to be of a cer­tain size before you can shoot it, it’s trophy hunting, pure and simple. Yes, these techniques work in some areas; it just bothers me that we are forced to adhere to those rules. Call me old­fashioned if you like, but I hanker for the good old days.

In a recent development, read Next: Why Do I Hunt? The Answer to Hunting’s Toughest Question.

It has been revealed that I wrote about this subject recently and a reader wrote back and called me a hypocrite. He said that I write for OUTDOOR LIFE and that this magazine endorses trophy-buck hunt­ing. Well, hellooooo. Show me a hunting magazine that doesn’t promote massive-buck hunting. There aren’t any. Show me a magazine with a forkhorn buck on the cover. There might have been one, once, but I never saw it.

It’s human nature to appreciate qual­ity. That’s why the Guinness Book of World Records and the Miss America pageant have such appeal. We admire the biggest, the best.

A hunter who gets a truly big buck, even when it’s total luck, becomes an instant hero. He endorses products, appears in ads, gives seminars and is a big name in hunting circles. The vast majority of these trophy owners just happened to be at the right place at the right time. Most did not “pattern” the buck, watching it for months before the season and discovering what trails it used. The lucky person was simply in the correct tree stand when the buck happened to walk by.

Whitetail hunting today is totally for­eign to what it was when I killed my first buck. In much of the country, farm­ing practices and more restrictive hunt­ing produces older bucks with larger antlers. High fences and nutritional supplements aren’t necessary in those places. Pals who live in the Midwest, for example, say that a few decades ago they never saw the likes of the bucks running around now. I’ve been hunting Iowa for years. The size of the bucks showing up these days is scary.

It has been revealed that all of us would like to shoot a major buck, myself included. Personally, I have a problem with antlers. When I see them, as long as they’re legal, the rifle is likely to swing up to my shoulder. There are exceptions, such as on a recent hunt in Kansas where I was told all sorts of 150-class bucks were waltzing around. I never saw one. I passed on plenty of other dandy bucks, ended up never firing a shot and cussed myself all the way home. Then there was the time in Saskatchewan, when a buck scoring 162 walked under my stand. It was pure dumb luck. I shot him, and I’m proud of him, and he’s my biggest buck ever, but I’m even more proud of a little six­pointer that hangs next to him.

Industry observers note that but that’s another story. As they say, a trophy is in the eye of the beholder. That’s the bottom line.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

Industry observers note that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

According to recent reports, eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

How to Soap-Tan a Rabbit Hide at Home

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that during the cold winter months, rabbit hunting is one of my favorite things to do.
  • Rabbit fur is incredibly soft and beautiful when it’s prime, and at the beginning of rabbit season this year I decided to start saving my rabbit hides to eventually make a blanket.
  • In a recent development, I knew that it would take quite a few rabbit pelts to create a blanket for anyone other than a baby, and sending them away to be professionally tanned would cost more than I wanted to spend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that during the cold winter months, rabbit hunting is one of my favorite things to do. Especially right after a fresh snow—there’s nothing like flinging arrows at cottontails.

Rabbit fur is incredibly soft and beautiful when it’s prime, and at the beginning of rabbit season this year I decided to start saving my rabbit hides to eventually make a blanket.

In a recent development, I knew that it would take quite a few rabbit pelts to create a blanket for anyone other than a baby, and sending them away to be professionally tanned would cost more than I wanted to spend. So, I decided to tan the rabbit hides on my own.

Industry observers note that I have tanned several deer hides, squirrels, fox, coyote, and mink. Rabbit, however, is a completely different story. If you’ve ever skinned a cottontail rabbit, you’ll know that their hides are the “tissue paper” of furbearing animals. Their skin is so thin and delicate that you can easily skin them without using a knife.

There are many ways to tan animal hides, and it can be overwhelming. Even once you decide on a specific method, there are various ways to approach it. After several nights of scouring the internet, including many taxidermy sites, I discovered a method called soap tanning that looked like it might work for rabbits. All the instructions I found were vague, but the process seemed simple enough. Not only does this method use simple household items, but it’s free of harsh chemicals. That means it’s safe to do indoors, and with small children and animals around.

Related: How to Butcher a Rabbit.

The whole process, excluding the drying, only took me about an hour from start to finish. It was very simple, and the hide came out beautifully. So, don’t toss those bunny furs next time you bag a few—save and tan them! You can tan the hides fresh, or put them in a Ziploc bag and freeze them until you’re ready to start the process. Thaw 24 hours prior to tanning.

The first step is probably the most difficult step because, as I noted above, rabbit hide is very thin and tears easily. Most hides are fleshed with a fleshing tool, but that doesn’t work for rabbit hides as it would destroy the thin skin. Working slowly is the best way to avoid tears, but if you do end up tearing the hide, it can be fixed later.

It has been revealed that place the hide fur-side down, flesh-side up on your board. Using the tacks (or nails, like I did) pin the rabbit hide to the board. You’ll want the hide to be taut, but don’t try to stretch it too much. Your hide may be an odd shape, but that’s okay. That will be fixed later, and it’s better to leave it oddly shaped for now.

According to recent reports, once the hide is in place, use the flat side of a butter knife to gently scrape up the layer of flesh from the hide. The flesh will be slightly pink, and the hide underneath will be black and white. Hold the knife horizontal, keeping it as parallel to the hide as much as possible.

Once you’ve scraped enough away, you can grab the flesh with your hands and slowly peel it back from the hide, a little at a time to prevent tearing. Once you do this a few times, this goes fairly quickly. Be extra careful around holes in the hide that have been left behind from bullets or broadheads.

Once all the flesh has been peeled from the hide, remove the nails from the hide, and remove the hide from the board.

Place the hide in a clean bowl or bucket, and add a cup of olive oil. The measurement isn’t really important; just add enough to saturate the hide. Using your hands, work the oil into the skin side (not the hair) until you see the skin start to turn translucent. Don’t worry if you get oil on the hair side, though, since you’ll wash it in the next step.

In another clean bowl or bucket, add enough room temperature water to submerge the hide completely.

Industry observers note that add a healthy dose of dish soap (I used roughly half of a bottle). Again, measurements aren’t extremely important, you just want a strong ratio of soap to water.

Sources indicate that using a large wooden spoon or your hands, gently stir the hide in the soap and water. I started with a spoon and found it easier to use my hands. Be careful not to stir too vigorously, as this will make any holes in the hide even bigger.

Recent findings suggest that keep stirring the hide until the skin side starts turning white. Once all areas have gone from translucent to white, you’re going to test a small piece.

Industry observers note that do this by bringing a small pot of water to a boil. Trim a small piece of the rabbit hide that’s roughly 2- x ½-inch. (This is a great way to use a ragged edge that you want to trim off to fix the shape.).

Drop it into the pot of boiling water and leave it for approximately 30 seconds. Then use tongs to remove the hide and let it rest on a towel for a second. If the hide curls and is stiff, add more soap to your soap and water solution, and continue stirring. If the hide comes out of the boiling water and is still soft and pliable, your soap tan is complete.

Take your hide out of the soap and water solution, and run it under room-temperature water until all the soap is gone. Gently squeeze the hide to remove as much excess water as possible.

According to recent reports, at this point, you’ll be able to trim the edges of your hide if you so choose. You’ll also want to sew any holes in the hide.

Sources indicate that cut a piece of thread about a foot long. Make a small knot in the one end of your thread, and thread the opposite end through your needle. You’ll want to use a simple whip stitch on the skin side to close the holes. Keep your stitches snug, but not so tight that the skin puckers. The edges of the hole should touch, but not overlap. This will result in smooth fur on the opposite side, with no lumps and bumps.

According to recent reports, this is the longest part of the process. It took roughly 24 hours for the rabbit hide to dry completely. You’ll want to keep it in a dry area, away from pets and make sure no mice or rodents can get to it.

Hanging it on a hook or draping it over a rack so air can get to both the skin and fur side will ensure even drying. The hide will probably shrink a bit as it dries, but this is normal.

You can soften the hide during the drying process, or after. Trying to stretch a rabbit hide just rips it in half, so simply folding it and rolling it into a ball is the easiest way to soften the hide and make it more supple. If you skip this step, however, your hide will still be extremely easy to work with if you are going to use it for a sewing project.

Recent findings suggest that the final step to tanning many hides is to smoke the hide over smoldering coals. Wet hides tend to dry stiff, even if they’ve been worked really well, and the smoke essentially “finishes” the hide in case it were ever to get water on it.

I chose to skip this step, as I blueprint on making a blanket once I have enough pelts, and it’s fairly unlikely that the blanket will ever get wet. On top of that, rabbit hides are so thin that even if they were to stiffen, they would still be very pliable.

In a recent development, if you do choose to smoke your rabbit hide, it only takes about 30 minutes. Keep in mind that smoking will change the color of the hide.

Read Next: Hunting Rabbits is the Perfect Cure for Winter Cabin Fever.

Recent findings suggest that decide what you want to do with the hide. The possibilities are endless, whether you choose to display the hide on an end table, create fur trim on a garment, or save a dozen to create a pillow or blanket.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a latest attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

It has been revealed that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

In a recent development, “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

Sources indicate that this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

Recent findings suggest that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

Latest Update: Foothills Trail Shakedown

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In November 2026, I took on the Foothills Trail (FHT) eastbound as my shakedown hike to test my gear, mental toughness, and physical strength.
  • Industry observers note that let’s talk about the gear I will NOT get rid of, my MVPs!
  • It has been revealed that the nights were cold with the lowest temp at camp being 28°F one night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In November 2026, I took on the Foothills Trail (FHT) eastbound as my shakedown hike to test my gear, mental toughness, and physical strength. Stretching 77 miles through North and South Carolina, the trail challenges hikers with rugged terrain. My watch had tracked 16,132 feet of ascent and 16,584 feet of descent. My main goal was simple: focus on what gear worked and what didn’t. It turned out to be the exact wake-up call I needed before January. Some of my systems passed with flying colors, while others forced an immediate rethink.

Industry observers note that let’s talk about the gear I will NOT get rid of, my MVPs! You can find a gear list breakdown in my profile. My tent is my favorite piece of gear by a long shot. Because it’s semi-freestanding, the poles give it structure, meaning I can pitch it practically anywhere with just a few stakes. It also weighs in at just under two pounds, which is a huge advantage. My second favorite piece of gear is my new down quilt. I’m naturally cold, so having a 20°F quilt hits the spot for chilly Florida winter temps and the late-season cold snaps of southern Appalachia. It has a closed footbox to keep my feet warm and pad straps, which clip underneath my sleeping pad to keep the quilt secured and trap warm air inside.

It has been revealed that the nights were cold with the lowest temp at camp being 28°F one night. At this time I had a 30°F quilt with an open toe box, no quilt straps, and by night two I had already decided this quilt wasn’t going to work even with my cold weather clothes. I sent many texts to my husband each night about how cold I was and even spent 45 minutes one night looking for a bail-out point for the following day which he wouldn’t learn until after my hike. Little did I know, he was one step ahead of me, as always, and had purchased a 20°F quilt for me after my first text night one. My first gear swap was complete before my shakedown trail had even really started.

More than any single piece of gear, the Foothills Trail taught me how vital it is to manage my body and timing. Taking time to stretch at the end of each day made a massive difference in keeping my muscles from locking up after hours of steep climbs and descents. I also realized that smart pacing isn’t just about hitting daily mileage goals. It’s about getting into camp with enough daylight to pitch my tent, eat dinner, and get into my warm layers before the temperature drops for the night. Walking away from those 77 miles, I feel way more confident in my gear.
